title: Introducing NV-Reason-CT Open 3D CT VLM for Radiologist Chain-of-Thought Reasoning | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA released NV-Reason-CT, an open 3D CT vision language model pairing a native 3D ViT encoder with Qwen3.5-4B, trained via SFT plus anatomy-aware GRPO to produce radiologist-style chain-of-thought and structured reports. It posts state-of-the-art CT-RATE results (Macro-F1 0.614, Macro-AUROC 0.871) versus VoxelFM, Pillar-0, CT-CLIP, Merlin and MedGemma 1.5, and is positioned as a post-trainable foundation for radiology AI vendors rather than a cleared clinical product.

insights.claim: 3D CT, one of the most data-dense imaging modalities, remains largely underserved by modern vision language models; frontier general-purpose models perform poorly on volumetric imaging and most open medical models lack multistep conversational depth.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Identifies a whitespace in medical imaging AI where specialized volumetric models can beat frontier generalists; relevant to radiology AI startups and imaging vendors.
insights.quote: Frontier general-purpose models perform poorly on volumetric imaging
insights.locator: Radiology AI has made remarkable strides

insights.claim: A single abdominal CT study can contain 300-600 axial slices, and treating it as independent 2D frames discards the inter-slice spatial relationships that define masses, effusions and infiltrates.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Explains why slice-based approaches (including frontier models) underperform, favoring native-3D architectures and higher compute per study.
insights.locator: Why 3D CT reasoning demands a different approach

insights.claim: Medical AI that outputs a diagnostic label without articulating its reasoning cannot be audited, taught from, or safely integrated into clinical workflows, so explainable chain-of-thought is framed as a prerequisite for clinical adoption.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Suggests explainability, not just accuracy, will gate adoption and regulatory acceptance of radiology AI; favors reasoning-capable models.
insights.quote: This is the kind of transparency that clinical adoption requires.

insights.claim: NV-Reason-CT combines the Qwen3.5-4B LLM with a Primus 3D ViT encoder initialized from Colipri weights, retrained end-to-end, processing 192^3-voxel volumes at 2 mm with 8x8x8 patches into 13,824 vision tokens passed unmerged to the LLM with 3D MRoPE positional encoding.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is building on an open Chinese base LLM (Qwen) for a flagship medical model; the large vision-token context implies meaningful inference compute per scan.

insights.claim: NV-Reason-CT is trained in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on about 550,000 structured QA examples (from CT-RATE, NIH CT datasets and CancerVerse plus LLM-distilled synthetic reasoning grounded on radiologist dictations), then GRPO reinforcement learning with an anatomy-aware reward.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: The SFT-then-RL recipe with synthetic distilled reasoning reduces the need for expensive expert annotation, lowering the cost of building domain reasoning models.
insights.locator: What is the NV-Reason-CT training methodology?

insights.claim: Rewarding accuracy per anatomical region rather than with a single global signal improves calibration across the chest-abdomen findings distribution and lets the model generalize without exhaustively annotated reasoning chains.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Structured, domain-decomposed RL rewards may be a transferable technique for vertical AI models in regulated fields.

insights.claim: NVIDIA curated a CT ontology of 30 chest and 29 abdominal abnormalities (including lung nodules, pneumothorax, hepatic lesions and renal cysts) to guide and evaluate NV-Reason-CT's structured reports.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Coverage of 60-ish findings in one pass is the basis for claimed reporting time savings.

insights.claim: On the CT-RATE benchmark (18 labels, fixed threshold), NV-Reason-CT scores Macro-F1 0.614 and Macro-AUROC 0.871, ahead of VoxelFM (0.581/0.870), Pillar-0 (0.544/0.861), ClinFusion-8B (0.442 F1), CT-CLIP (0.398/0.733), Merlin (0.358/0.662) and MedGemma 1.5 (0.303 F1).
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's open model roughly doubles Google's MedGemma 1.5 on F1, putting pressure on competing medical foundation models; AUROC lead over VoxelFM is marginal.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims NV-Reason-CT is the first single open model to achieve competitive CT classification and report generation simultaneously, evaluated with a plain Yes/No prompt and no classification head or task-specific adaptation.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Generative VLMs matching or beating contrastive/discriminative models on classification suggests consolidation of radiology AI onto generalist generative backbones.
insights.quote: This is the first time a single open model has achieved competitive CT classification and report generation simultaneously.
insights.locator: On CT-RATE, the primary public benchmark

insights.claim: NIH radiologists reviewed NV-Reason-CT and validated the quality of its structured reports and the clinical plausibility of its reasoning traces; the predecessor NV-Reason-CXR methodology was validated in a multireader study accepted at RSNA 2026 showing radiologist time savings without loss of diagnostic accuracy.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Clinical validation evidence is accumulating for NVIDIA's reasoning approach, a step toward productization by partners.
insights.quote: Being able to review the model’s thought process—not just its conclusions—is what makes it possible to trust and act on its findings.

insights.claim: NV-Reason-CT is released as an open research foundation for post-training, explicitly not an autonomous diagnostic system or cleared clinical product, with checkpoints on Hugging Face and post-training recipes on GitHub.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: NVIDIA avoids regulatory exposure and leaves FDA clearance and monetization to partners, while seeding demand for its compute.
insights.quote: not an autonomous diagnostic system or a cleared clinical product
insights.locator: NV-Reason-CT is an open research and development foundation

insights.claim: NVIDIA names Aidoc, HOPPR, Rad AI, Mosaic Clinical Technologies and Raidium as companies in spaces where an open conversational 3D CT model addresses a capability gap, alongside radiology workflow vendors, PACS developers and clinical decision support platforms.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Watchlist of radiology AI companies likely to build on NVIDIA's open models; open foundations may lower their R&D costs but also lower barriers for competitors.
insights.locator: Medical AI companies including radiology workflow vendors

insights.claim: NV-Reason-CT is part of an NVIDIA Medical AI family (NV-Generate-CTMR for synthetic CT/MRI, NV-Segment-CTMR for segmentation, NV-Reason-CXR for chest X-ray) intended to form end-to-end radiology pipelines from synthetic data to conversational reasoning.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is building a full-stack open healthcare model portfolio, expanding its platform role in medical imaging beyond hardware.
insights.locator: How NV-Reason-CT fits within the NVIDIA Medical AI ecosystem

insights.claim: NV-Reason-CT produces a structured report covering 60+ abnormalities in seconds, which clinicians can scan, validate and amend, reducing cognitive load of routine reporting while keeping radiologist oversight.
insights.speaker: Andriy Myronenko
insights.so_what: Radiologist productivity gains are the core ROI argument for hospital adoption of reasoning-based imaging AI.
